  42 def _make_inset_locator(bounds, trans, parent): 
  43     """ 
  44     Helper function to locate inset axes, used in 
  45     `.Axes.inset_axes`. 
  46  
  47     A locator gets used in `Axes.set_aspect` to override the default 
  48     locations...  It is a function that takes an axes object and 
  49     a renderer and tells `set_aspect` where it is to be placed. 
  50  
  51     Here *rect* is a rectangle [l, b, w, h] that specifies the 
  52     location for the axes in the transform given by *trans* on the 
  53     *parent*. 
  54     """ 
  55     _bounds = mtransforms.Bbox.from_bounds(*bounds) 
  56     _trans = trans 
  57     _parent = parent 
  58  
  59     def inset_locator(ax, renderer): 
  60         bbox = _bounds 
  61         bb = mtransforms.TransformedBbox(bbox, _trans) 
  62         tr = _parent.figure.transFigure.inverted() 
  63         bb = mtransforms.TransformedBbox(bb, tr) 
  64         return bb 
  65  
  66     return inset_locator

  69 # The axes module contains all the wrappers to plotting functions.

  73 class Axes(_AxesBase): 
  74     """ 
  75     The `Axes` contains most of the figure elements: `~.axis.Axis`, 
  76     `~.axis.Tick`, `~.lines.Line2D`, `~.text.Text`, `~.patches.Polygon`, etc., 
  77     and sets the coordinate system. 
  78  
  79     The `Axes` instance supports callbacks through a callbacks attribute which 
  80     is a `~.cbook.CallbackRegistry` instance.  The events you can connect to 
  81     are 'xlim_changed' and 'ylim_changed' and the callback will be called with 
  82     func(*ax*) where *ax* is the `Axes` instance. 
  83  
  84     Attributes 
  85     ---------- 
  86     dataLim : `.Bbox` 
  87         The bounding box enclosing all data displayed in the Axes. 
  88     viewLim : `.Bbox` 
  89         The view limits in data coordinates. 
  90  
  91     """ 
  92     ### Labelling, legend and texts 
  93

  97         return 'Axes'

  99     def get_title(self, loc="center"): 
 100         """ 
 101         Get an axes title. 
 102  
 103         Get one of the three available axes titles. The available titles 
 104         are positioned above the axes in the center, flush with the left 
 105         edge, and flush with the right edge. 
 106  
 107         Parameters 
 108         ---------- 
 109         loc : {'center', 'left', 'right'}, str, default: 'center' 
 110             Which title to return. 
 111  
 112         Returns 
 113         ------- 
 114         title : str 
 115             The title text string. 
 116  
 117         """ 
 118         titles = {'left': self._left_title, 
 119                   'center': self.title, 
 120                   'right': self._right_title} 
 121         title = cbook._check_getitem(titles, loc=loc.lower()) 
 122         return title.get_text() 
 123  
 124     def set_title(self, label, fontdict=None, loc=None, pad=None, 
 125                     **kwargs): 
 126         """ 
 127         Set a title for the axes. 
 128  
 129         Set one of the three available axes titles. The available titles 
 130         are positioned above the axes in the center, flush with the left 
 131         edge, and flush with the right edge. 
 132  
 133         Parameters 
 134         ---------- 
 135         label : str 
 136             Text to use for the title 
 137  
 138         fontdict : dict 
 139             A dictionary controlling the appearance of the title text, 
 140             the default *fontdict* is:: 
 141  
 142                {'fontsize': rcParams['axes.titlesize'], 
 143                 'fontweight' : rcParams['axes.titleweight'], 
 144                 'color' : rcParams['axes.titlecolor'], 
 145                 'verticalalignment': 'baseline', 
 146                 'horizontalalignment': loc} 
 147  
 148         loc : {'center', 'left', 'right'}, str, optional 
 149             Which title to set. 
 150             If *None*, defaults to :rc:`axes.titlelocation`. 
 151  
 152         pad : float 
 153             The offset of the title from the top of the axes, in points. 
 154             If *None*, defaults to :rc:`axes.titlepad`. 
 155  
 156         Returns 
 157         ------- 
 158         text : :class:`~matplotlib.text.Text` 
 159             The matplotlib text instance representing the title 
 160  
 161         Other Parameters 
 162         ---------------- 
 163         **kwargs : `~matplotlib.text.Text` properties 
 164             Other keyword arguments are text properties, see 
 165             :class:`~matplotlib.text.Text` for a list of valid text 
 166             properties. 
 167         """ 
 168         if loc is None: 
 169             loc = rcParams['axes.titlelocation'] 
 170  
 171         titles = {'left': self._left_title, 
 172                   'center': self.title, 
 173                   'right': self._right_title} 
 174         title = cbook._check_getitem(titles, loc=loc.lower()) 
 175         default = { 
 176             'fontsize': rcParams['axes.titlesize'], 
 177             'fontweight': rcParams['axes.titleweight'], 
 178             'verticalalignment': 'baseline', 
 179             'horizontalalignment': loc.lower()} 
 180         titlecolor = rcParams['axes.titlecolor'] 
 181         if not cbook._str_lower_equal(titlecolor, 'auto'): 
 182             default["color"] = titlecolor 
 183         if pad is None: 
 184             pad = rcParams['axes.titlepad'] 
 185         self._set_title_offset_trans(float(pad)) 
 186         title.set_text(label) 
 187         title.update(default) 
 188         if fontdict is not None: 
 189             title.update(fontdict) 
 190         title.update(kwargs) 
 191         return title

 276     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
 277     def legend(self, *args, **kwargs): 
 278         """ 
 279         Place a legend on the axes. 
 280  
 281         Call signatures:: 
 282  
 283             legend() 
 284             legend(labels) 
 285             legend(handles, labels) 
 286  
 287         The call signatures correspond to three different ways how to use 
 288         this method. 
 289  
 290         **1. Automatic detection of elements to be shown in the legend** 
 291  
 292         The elements to be added to the legend are automatically determined, 
 293         when you do not pass in any extra arguments. 
 294  
 295         In this case, the labels are taken from the artist. You can specify 
 296         them either at artist creation or by calling the 
 297         :meth:`~.Artist.set_label` method on the artist:: 
 298  
 299             line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3], label='Inline label') 
 300             ax.legend() 
 301  
 302         or:: 
 303  
 304             line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3]) 
 305             line.set_label('Label via method') 
 306             ax.legend() 
 307  
 308         Specific lines can be excluded from the automatic legend element 
 309         selection by defining a label starting with an underscore. 
 310         This is default for all artists, so calling `Axes.legend` without 
 311         any arguments and without setting the labels manually will result in 
 312         no legend being drawn. 
 313  
 314  
 315         **2. Labeling existing plot elements** 
 316  
 317         To make a legend for lines which already exist on the axes 
 318         (via plot for instance), simply call this function with an iterable 
 319         of strings, one for each legend item. For example:: 
 320  
 321             ax.plot([1, 2, 3]) 
 322             ax.legend(['A simple line']) 
 323  
 324         Note: This way of using is discouraged, because the relation between 
 325         plot elements and labels is only implicit by their order and can 
 326         easily be mixed up. 
 327  
 328  
 329         **3. Explicitly defining the elements in the legend** 
 330  
 331         For full control of which artists have a legend entry, it is possible 
 332         to pass an iterable of legend artists followed by an iterable of 
 333         legend labels respectively:: 
 334  
 335             legend((line1, line2, line3), ('label1', 'label2', 'label3')) 
 336  
 337         Parameters 
 338         ---------- 
 339         handles : sequence of `.Artist`, optional 
 340             A list of Artists (lines, patches) to be added to the legend. 
 341             Use this together with *labels*, if you need full control on what 
 342             is shown in the legend and the automatic mechanism described above 
 343             is not sufficient. 
 344  
 345             The length of handles and labels should be the same in this 
 346             case. If they are not, they are truncated to the smaller length. 
 347  
 348         labels : list of str, optional 
 349             A list of labels to show next to the artists. 
 350             Use this together with *handles*, if you need full control on what 
 351             is shown in the legend and the automatic mechanism described above 
 352             is not sufficient. 
 353  
 354         Other Parameters 
 355         ---------------- 
 356         %(_legend_kw_doc)s 
 357  
 358         Returns 
 359         ------- 
 360         legend : `~matplotlib.legend.Legend` 
 361  
 362         Notes 
 363         ----- 
 364         Not all kinds of artist are supported by the legend command. See 
 365         :doc:`/tutorials/intermediate/legend_guide` for details. 
 366  
 367         Examples 
 368         -------- 
 369         .. plot:: gallery/text_labels_and_annotations/legend.py 
 370         """ 
 371         handles, labels, extra_args, kwargs = mlegend._parse_legend_args( 
 372                 [self], 
 373                 *args, 
 374                 **kwargs) 
 375         if len(extra_args): 
 376             raise TypeError('legend only accepts two non-keyword arguments') 
 377         self.legend_ = mlegend.Legend(self, handles, labels, **kwargs) 
 378         self.legend_._remove_method = self._remove_legend 
 379         return self.legend_ 
 380  
 381     def _remove_legend(self, legend): 
 382         self.legend_ = None

 384     def inset_axes(self, bounds, *, transform=None, zorder=5, **kwargs): 
 385         """ 
 386         Add a child inset axes to this existing axes. 
 387  
 388         Warnings 
 389         -------- 
 390         This method is experimental as of 3.0, and the API may change. 
 391  
 392         Parameters 
 393         ---------- 
 394         bounds : [x0, y0, width, height] 
 395             Lower-left corner of inset axes, and its width and height. 
 396  
 397         transform : `.Transform` 
 398             Defaults to `ax.transAxes`, i.e. the units of *rect* are in 
 399             axes-relative coordinates. 
 400  
 401         zorder : number 
 402             Defaults to 5 (same as `.Axes.legend`).  Adjust higher or lower 
 403             to change whether it is above or below data plotted on the 
 404             parent axes. 
 405  
 406         **kwargs 
 407             Other keyword arguments are passed on to the `.Axes` child axes. 
 408  
 409         Returns 
 410         ------- 
 411         ax 
 412             The created `~.axes.Axes` instance. 
 413  
 414         Examples 
 415         -------- 
 416         This example makes two inset axes, the first is in axes-relative 
 417         coordinates, and the second in data-coordinates:: 
 418  
 419             fig, ax = plt.subplots() 
 420             ax.plot(range(10)) 
 421             axin1 = ax.inset_axes([0.8, 0.1, 0.15, 0.15]) 
 422             axin2 = ax.inset_axes( 
 423                     [5, 7, 2.3, 2.3], transform=ax.transData) 
 424  
 425         """ 
 426         if transform is None: 
 427             transform = self.transAxes 
 428         label = kwargs.pop('label', 'inset_axes') 
 429  
 430         # This puts the rectangle into figure-relative coordinates. 
 431         inset_locator = _make_inset_locator(bounds, transform, self) 
 432         bb = inset_locator(None, None) 
 433  
 434         inset_ax = Axes(self.figure, bb.bounds, zorder=zorder, 
 435                 label=label, **kwargs) 
 436  
 437         # this locator lets the axes move if in data coordinates. 
 438         # it gets called in `ax.apply_aspect() (of all places) 
 439         inset_ax.set_axes_locator(inset_locator) 
 440  
 441         self.add_child_axes(inset_ax) 
 442  
 443         return inset_ax

 445     def indicate_inset(self, bounds, inset_ax=None, *, transform=None, 
 446             facecolor='none', edgecolor='0.5', alpha=0.5, 
 447             zorder=4.99, **kwargs): 
 448         """ 
 449         Add an inset indicator to the axes.  This is a rectangle on the plot 
 450         at the position indicated by *bounds* that optionally has lines that 
 451         connect the rectangle to an inset axes (`.Axes.inset_axes`). 
 452  
 453         Warnings 
 454         -------- 
 455         This method is experimental as of 3.0, and the API may change. 
 456  
 457  
 458         Parameters 
 459         ---------- 
 460         bounds : [x0, y0, width, height] 
 461             Lower-left corner of rectangle to be marked, and its width 
 462             and height. 
 463  
 464         inset_ax : `.Axes` 
 465             An optional inset axes to draw connecting lines to.  Two lines are 
 466             drawn connecting the indicator box to the inset axes on corners 
 467             chosen so as to not overlap with the indicator box. 
 468  
 469         transform : `.Transform` 
 470             Transform for the rectangle co-ordinates. Defaults to 
 471             `ax.transAxes`, i.e. the units of *rect* are in axes-relative 
 472             coordinates. 
 473  
 474         facecolor : color, default: 'none' 
 475             Facecolor of the rectangle. 
 476  
 477         edgecolor : color, default: '0.5' 
 478             Color of the rectangle and color of the connecting lines. 
 479  
 480         alpha : float 
 481             Transparency of the rectangle and connector lines.  Default is 0.5. 
 482  
 483         zorder : float 
 484             Drawing order of the rectangle and connector lines. Default is 4.99 
 485             (just below the default level of inset axes). 
 486  
 487         **kwargs 
 488             Other keyword arguments are passed on to the rectangle patch. 
 489  
 490         Returns 
 491         ------- 
 492         rectangle_patch : `.patches.Rectangle` 
 493              The indicator frame. 
 494  
 495         connector_lines : 4-tuple of `.patches.ConnectionPatch` 
 496             The four connector lines connecting to (lower_left, upper_left, 
 497             lower_right upper_right) corners of *inset_ax*. Two lines are 
 498             set with visibility to *False*,  but the user can set the 
 499             visibility to True if the automatic choice is not deemed correct. 
 500  
 501         """ 
 502         # to make the axes connectors work, we need to apply the aspect to 
 503         # the parent axes. 
 504         self.apply_aspect() 
 505  
 506         if transform is None: 
 507             transform = self.transData 
 508         label = kwargs.pop('label', 'indicate_inset') 
 509  
 510         x, y, width, height = bounds 
 511         rectangle_patch = mpatches.Rectangle( 
 512             (x, y), width, height, 
 513             facecolor=facecolor, edgecolor=edgecolor, alpha=alpha, 
 514             zorder=zorder,  label=label, transform=transform, **kwargs) 
 515         self.add_patch(rectangle_patch) 
 516  
 517         connects = [] 
 518  
 519         if inset_ax is not None: 
 520             # connect the inset_axes to the rectangle 
 521             for xy_inset_ax in [(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)]: 
 522                 # inset_ax positions are in axes coordinates 
 523                 # The 0, 1 values define the four edges if the inset_ax 
 524                 # lower_left, upper_left, lower_right upper_right. 
 525                 ex, ey = xy_inset_ax 
 526                 if self.xaxis.get_inverted(): 
 527                     ex = 1 - ex 
 528                 if self.yaxis.get_inverted(): 
 529                     ey = 1 - ey 
 530                 xy_data = x + ex * width, y + ey * height 
 531                 p = mpatches.ConnectionPatch( 
 532                     xyA=xy_inset_ax, coordsA=inset_ax.transAxes, 
 533                     xyB=xy_data, coordsB=self.transData, 
 534                     arrowstyle="-", zorder=zorder, 
 535                     edgecolor=edgecolor, alpha=alpha) 
 536                 connects.append(p) 
 537                 self.add_patch(p) 
 538  
 539             # decide which two of the lines to keep visible.... 
 540             pos = inset_ax.get_position() 
 541             bboxins = pos.transformed(self.figure.transFigure) 
 542             rectbbox = mtransforms.Bbox.from_bounds( 
 543                 *bounds 
 544             ).transformed(transform) 
 545             x0 = rectbbox.x0 < bboxins.x0 
 546             x1 = rectbbox.x1 < bboxins.x1 
 547             y0 = rectbbox.y0 < bboxins.y0 
 548             y1 = rectbbox.y1 < bboxins.y1 
 549             connects[0].set_visible(x0 ^ y0) 
 550             connects[1].set_visible(x0 == y1) 
 551             connects[2].set_visible(x1 == y0) 
 552             connects[3].set_visible(x1 ^ y1) 
 553  
 554         return rectangle_patch, tuple(connects) if connects else None 
 555  
 556     def indicate_inset_zoom(self, inset_ax, **kwargs): 
 557         """ 
 558         Add an inset indicator rectangle to the axes based on the axis 
 559         limits for an *inset_ax* and draw connectors between *inset_ax* 
 560         and the rectangle. 
 561  
 562         Warnings 
 563         -------- 
 564         This method is experimental as of 3.0, and the API may change. 
 565  
 566         Parameters 
 567         ---------- 
 568         inset_ax : `.Axes` 
 569             Inset axes to draw connecting lines to.  Two lines are 
 570             drawn connecting the indicator box to the inset axes on corners 
 571             chosen so as to not overlap with the indicator box. 
 572  
 573         **kwargs 
 574             Other keyword arguments are passed on to `.Axes.indicate_inset` 
 575  
 576         Returns 
 577         ------- 
 578         rectangle_patch : `.Patches.Rectangle` 
 579              Rectangle artist. 
 580  
 581         connector_lines : 4-tuple of `.Patches.ConnectionPatch` 
 582             Each of four connector lines coming from the rectangle drawn on 
 583             this axis, in the order lower left, upper left, lower right, 
 584             upper right. 
 585             Two are set with visibility to *False*,  but the user can 
 586             set the visibility to *True* if the automatic choice is not deemed 
 587             correct. 
 588         """ 
 589  
 590         xlim = inset_ax.get_xlim() 
 591         ylim = inset_ax.get_ylim() 
 592         rect = (xlim[0], ylim[0], xlim[1] - xlim[0], ylim[1] - ylim[0]) 
 593         return self.indicate_inset(rect, inset_ax, **kwargs)

 595     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
 596     def secondary_xaxis(self, location, *, functions=None, **kwargs): 
 597         """ 
 598         Add a second x-axis to this axes. 
 599  
 600         For example if we want to have a second scale for the data plotted on 
 601         the xaxis. 
 602  
 603         %(_secax_docstring)s 
 604  
 605         Examples 
 606         -------- 
 607         The main axis shows frequency, and the secondary axis shows period. 
 608  
 609         .. plot:: 
 610  
 611             fig, ax = plt.subplots() 
 612             ax.loglog(range(1, 360, 5), range(1, 360, 5)) 
 613             ax.set_xlabel('frequency [Hz]') 
 614  
 615             def invert(x): 
 616                 return 1 / x 
 617  
 618             secax = ax.secondary_xaxis('top', functions=(invert, invert)) 
 619             secax.set_xlabel('Period [s]') 
 620             plt.show() 
 621         """ 
 622         if (location in ['top', 'bottom'] or isinstance(location, Number)): 
 623             secondary_ax = SecondaryAxis(self, 'x', location, functions, 
 624                                          **kwargs) 
 625             self.add_child_axes(secondary_ax) 
 626             return secondary_ax 
 627         else: 
 628             raise ValueError('secondary_xaxis location must be either ' 
 629                              'a float or "top"/"bottom"') 
 630  
 631     def secondary_yaxis(self, location, *, functions=None, **kwargs): 
 632         """ 
 633         Add a second y-axis to this axes. 
 634  
 635         For example if we want to have a second scale for the data plotted on 
 636         the yaxis. 
 637  
 638         %(_secax_docstring)s 
 639  
 640         Examples 
 641         -------- 
 642         Add a secondary axes that converts from radians to degrees 
 643  
 644         .. plot:: 
 645  
 646             fig, ax = plt.subplots() 
 647             ax.plot(range(1, 360, 5), range(1, 360, 5)) 
 648             ax.set_ylabel('degrees') 
 649             secax = ax.secondary_yaxis('right', functions=(np.deg2rad, 
 650                                                            np.rad2deg)) 
 651             secax.set_ylabel('radians') 
 652         """ 
 653         if location in ['left', 'right'] or isinstance(location, Number): 
 654             secondary_ax = SecondaryAxis(self, 'y', location, 
 655                                          functions, **kwargs) 
 656             self.add_child_axes(secondary_ax) 
 657             return secondary_ax 
 658         else: 
 659             raise ValueError('secondary_yaxis location must be either ' 
 660                              'a float or "left"/"right"')

 662     @cbook._delete_parameter("3.1", "withdash") 
 663     def text(self, x, y, s, fontdict=None, withdash=False, **kwargs): 
 664         """ 
 665         Add text to the axes. 
 666  
 667         Add the text *s* to the axes at location *x*, *y* in data coordinates. 
 668  
 669         Parameters 
 670         ---------- 
 671         x, y : scalars 
 672             The position to place the text. By default, this is in data 
 673             coordinates. The coordinate system can be changed using the 
 674             *transform* parameter. 
 675  
 676         s : str 
 677             The text. 
 678  
 679         fontdict : dict, default: None 
 680             A dictionary to override the default text properties. If fontdict 
 681             is None, the defaults are determined by your rc parameters. 
 682  
 683         withdash : bool, default: False 
 684             Creates a `~matplotlib.text.TextWithDash` instance instead of a 
 685             `~matplotlib.text.Text` instance. 
 686  
 687         Returns 
 688         ------- 
 689         text : `.Text` 
 690             The created `.Text` instance. 
 691  
 692         Other Parameters 
 693         ---------------- 
 694         **kwargs : `~matplotlib.text.Text` properties. 
 695             Other miscellaneous text parameters. 
 696  
 697         Examples 
 698         -------- 
 699         Individual keyword arguments can be used to override any given 
 700         parameter:: 
 701  
 702             >>> text(x, y, s, fontsize=12) 
 703  
 704         The default transform specifies that text is in data coords, 
 705         alternatively, you can specify text in axis coords ((0, 0) is 
 706         lower-left and (1, 1) is upper-right).  The example below places 
 707         text in the center of the axes:: 
 708  
 709             >>> text(0.5, 0.5, 'matplotlib', horizontalalignment='center', 
 710             ...      verticalalignment='center', transform=ax.transAxes) 
 711  
 712         You can put a rectangular box around the text instance (e.g., to 
 713         set a background color) by using the keyword *bbox*.  *bbox* is 
 714         a dictionary of `~matplotlib.patches.Rectangle` 
 715         properties.  For example:: 
 716  
 717             >>> text(x, y, s, bbox=dict(facecolor='red', alpha=0.5)) 
 718         """ 
 719         if fontdict is None: 
 720             fontdict = {} 
 721  
 722         effective_kwargs = { 
 723             'verticalalignment': 'baseline', 
 724             'horizontalalignment': 'left', 
 725             'transform': self.transData, 
 726             'clip_on': False, 
 727             **fontdict, 
 728             **kwargs, 
 729         } 
 730  
 731         # At some point if we feel confident that TextWithDash 
 732         # is robust as a drop-in replacement for Text and that 
 733         # the performance impact of the heavier-weight class 
 734         # isn't too significant, it may make sense to eliminate 
 735         # the withdash kwarg and simply delegate whether there's 
 736         # a dash to TextWithDash and dashlength. 
 737  
 738         if (withdash 
 739                 and withdash is not cbook.deprecation._deprecated_parameter): 
 740             t = mtext.TextWithDash(x, y, text=s) 
 741         else: 
 742             t = mtext.Text(x, y, text=s) 
 743         t.update(effective_kwargs) 
 744  
 745         t.set_clip_path(self.patch) 
 746         self._add_text(t) 
 747         return t

 797         -------- 
 798         * draw a thick red hline at 'y' = 0 that spans the xrange:: 
 799  
 800             >>> axhline(linewidth=4, color='r') 
 801  
 802         * draw a default hline at 'y' = 1 that spans the xrange:: 
 803

 807           the xrange::

 814                 + "axhline generates its own transform.")

 818         # non-unitized bounds 
 819         self._process_unit_info(ydata=y, kwargs=kwargs) 
 820         yy = self.convert_yunits(y)

 824         l = mlines.Line2D([xmin, xmax], [y, y], transform=trans, **kwargs) 
 825         self.add_line(l)

 900     def axline(self, xy1, xy2, **kwargs): 
 901         """ 
 902         Add an infinitely long straight line that passes through two points. 
 903  
 904         This draws a straight line "on the screen", regardless of the x and y 
 905         scales, and is thus also suitable for drawing exponential decays in 
 906         semilog plots, power laws in loglog plots, etc. 
 907  
 908         Parameters 
 909         ---------- 
 910         xy1, xy2 : (float, float) 
 911             Points for the line to pass through. 
 912  
 913         Returns 
 914         ------- 
 915         :class:`~matplotlib.lines.Line2D` 
 916  
 917         Other Parameters 
 918         ---------------- 
 919         **kwargs 
 920             Valid kwargs are :class:`~matplotlib.lines.Line2D` properties, 
 921             with the exception of 'transform': 
 922  
 923             %(_Line2D_docstr)s 
 924  
 925         Examples 
 926         -------- 
 927         Draw a thick red line passing through (0, 0) and (1, 1):: 
 928  
 929             >>> axline((0, 0), (1, 1), linewidth=4, color='r') 
 930  
 931         See Also 
 932         -------- 
 933         axhline : for horizontal lines 
 934         axvline : for vertical lines 
 935         """ 
 936  
 937         if "transform" in kwargs: 
 938             raise TypeError("'transform' is not allowed as a kwarg; " 
 939                             "axline generates its own transform") 
 940         x1, y1 = xy1 
 941         x2, y2 = xy2 
 942         line = mlines._AxLine([x1, x2], [y1, y2], **kwargs) 
 943         # Like add_line, but correctly handling data limits. 
 944         self._set_artist_props(line) 
 945         if line.get_clip_path() is None: 
 946             line.set_clip_path(self.patch) 
 947         if not line.get_label(): 
 948             line.set_label(f"_line{len(self.lines)}") 
 949         self.lines.append(line) 
 950         line._remove_method = self.lines.remove 
 951         self.update_datalim([xy1, xy2]) 
 952  
 953         self._request_autoscale_view() 
 954         return line

 956     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
 957     def axhspan(self, ymin, ymax, xmin=0, xmax=1, **kwargs): 
 958         """ 
 959         Add a horizontal span (rectangle) across the axis. 
 960  
 961         Draw a horizontal span (rectangle) from *ymin* to *ymax*. 
 962         With the default values of *xmin* = 0 and *xmax* = 1, this 
 963         always spans the xrange, regardless of the xlim settings, even 
 964         if you change them, e.g., with the :meth:`set_xlim` command. 
 965         That is, the horizontal extent is in axes coords: 0=left, 
 966         0.5=middle, 1.0=right but the *y* location is in data 
 967         coordinates. 
 968  
 969         Parameters 
 970         ---------- 
 971         ymin : float 
 972             Lower y-coordinate of the span, in data units. 
 973         ymax : float 
 974             Upper y-coordinate of the span, in data units. 
 975         xmin : float, default: 0 
 976             Lower x-coordinate of the span, in x-axis (0-1) units. 
 977         xmax : float, default: 1 
 978             Upper x-coordinate of the span, in x-axis (0-1) units. 
 979  
 980         Returns 
 981         ------- 
 982         Polygon : `~matplotlib.patches.Polygon` 
 983  
 984         Other Parameters 
 985         ---------------- 
 986         **kwargs : `~matplotlib.patches.Polygon` properties. 
 987  
 988         %(Polygon)s 
 989  
 990         See Also 
 991         -------- 
 992         axvspan : Add a vertical span across the axes. 
 993         """ 
 994         trans = self.get_yaxis_transform(which='grid') 
 995  
 996         # process the unit information 
 997         self._process_unit_info([xmin, xmax], [ymin, ymax], kwargs=kwargs) 
 998  
 999         # first we need to strip away the units 
1000         xmin, xmax = self.convert_xunits([xmin, xmax]) 
1001         ymin, ymax = self.convert_yunits([ymin, ymax]) 
1002  
1003         verts = (xmin, ymin), (xmin, ymax), (xmax, ymax), (xmax, ymin) 
1004         p = mpatches.Polygon(verts, **kwargs) 
1005         p.set_transform(trans) 
1006         self.add_patch(p) 
1007         self._request_autoscale_view(scalex=False) 
1008         return p

1010     def axvspan(self, xmin, xmax, ymin=0, ymax=1, **kwargs): 
1011         """ 
1012         Add a vertical span (rectangle) across the axes. 
1013  
1014         Draw a vertical span (rectangle) from *xmin* to *xmax*.  With 
1015         the default values of *ymin* = 0 and *ymax* = 1. This always 
1016         spans the yrange, regardless of the ylim settings, even if you 
1017         change them, e.g., with the :meth:`set_ylim` command.  That is, 
1018         the vertical extent is in axes coords: 0=bottom, 0.5=middle, 
1019         1.0=top but the x location is in data coordinates.

1032         Returns 
1033         -------

1035             Vertical span (rectangle) from (xmin, ymin) to (xmax, ymax).

1049         x = 1.55 that spans the yrange of the axes.

1052  
1053         """ 
1054         trans = self.get_xaxis_transform(which='grid') 
1055  
1056         # process the unit information 
1057         self._process_unit_info([xmin, xmax], [ymin, ymax], kwargs=kwargs)

1064         p = mpatches.Polygon(verts, **kwargs)

1066         self.add_patch(p) 
1067         self._request_autoscale_view(scaley=False)

1070     @_preprocess_data(replace_names=["y", "xmin", "xmax", "colors"], 
1071                       label_namer="y") 
1072     def hlines(self, y, xmin, xmax, colors='k', linestyles='solid', 
1073                label='', **kwargs): 
1074         """ 
1075         Plot horizontal lines at each *y* from *xmin* to *xmax*. 
1076  
1077         Parameters 
1078         ---------- 
1079         y : scalar or sequence of scalar 
1080             y-indexes where to plot the lines. 
1081  
1082         xmin, xmax : scalar or 1D array-like 
1083             Respective beginning and end of each line. If scalars are 
1084             provided, all lines will have same length. 
1085  
1086         colors : array-like of colors, default: 'k' 
1087  
1088         linestyles : {'solid', 'dashed', 'dashdot', 'dotted'}, optional 
1089  
1090         label : str, default: '' 
1091  
1092         Returns 
1093         ------- 
1094         lines : `~matplotlib.collections.LineCollection` 
1095  
1096         Other Parameters 
1097         ---------------- 
1098         **kwargs :  `~matplotlib.collections.LineCollection` properties. 
1099  
1100         See also 
1101         -------- 
1102         vlines : vertical lines 
1103         axhline: horizontal line across the axes 
1104         """ 
1105  
1106         # We do the conversion first since not all unitized data is uniform 
1107         # process the unit information 
1108         self._process_unit_info([xmin, xmax], y, kwargs=kwargs) 
1109         y = self.convert_yunits(y) 
1110         xmin = self.convert_xunits(xmin) 
1111         xmax = self.convert_xunits(xmax) 
1112  
1113         if not np.iterable(y): 
1114             y = [y] 
1115         if not np.iterable(xmin): 
1116             xmin = [xmin] 
1117         if not np.iterable(xmax): 
1118             xmax = [xmax] 
1119  
1120         y, xmin, xmax = cbook.delete_masked_points(y, xmin, xmax) 
1121  
1122         y = np.ravel(y) 
1123         xmin = np.resize(xmin, y.shape) 
1124         xmax = np.resize(xmax, y.shape) 
1125  
1126         verts = [((thisxmin, thisy), (thisxmax, thisy)) 
1127                  for thisxmin, thisxmax, thisy in zip(xmin, xmax, y)] 
1128         lines = mcoll.LineCollection(verts, colors=colors, 
1129                                      linestyles=linestyles, label=label) 
1130         self.add_collection(lines, autolim=False) 
1131         lines.update(kwargs) 
1132  
1133         if len(y) > 0: 
1134             minx = min(xmin.min(), xmax.min()) 
1135             maxx = max(xmin.max(), xmax.max()) 
1136             miny = y.min() 
1137             maxy = y.max() 
1138  
1139             corners = (minx, miny), (maxx, maxy) 
1140  
1141             self.update_datalim(corners) 
1142             self._request_autoscale_view() 
1143  
1144         return lines

1148     def vlines(self, x, ymin, ymax, colors='k', linestyles='solid', 
1149                label='', **kwargs): 
1150         """ 
1151         Plot vertical lines. 
1152  
1153         Plot vertical lines at each *x* from *ymin* to *ymax*. 
1154  
1155         Parameters 
1156         ---------- 
1157         x : scalar or 1D array-like 
1158             x-indexes where to plot the lines. 
1159  
1160         ymin, ymax : scalar or 1D array-like 
1161             Respective beginning and end of each line. If scalars are 
1162             provided, all lines will have same length. 
1163  
1164         colors : array-like of colors, default: 'k' 
1165  
1166         linestyles : {'solid', 'dashed', 'dashdot', 'dotted'}, optional 
1167  
1168         label : str, default: ''

1171         ------- 
1172         lines : `~matplotlib.collections.LineCollection`

1175         ---------------- 
1176         **kwargs : `~matplotlib.collections.LineCollection` properties. 
1177  
1178         See also 
1179         -------- 
1180         hlines : horizontal lines 
1181         axvline: vertical line across the axes 
1182         """ 
1183  
1184         self._process_unit_info(xdata=x, ydata=[ymin, ymax], kwargs=kwargs) 
1185  
1186         # We do the conversion first since not all unitized data is uniform 
1187         x = self.convert_xunits(x) 
1188         ymin = self.convert_yunits(ymin) 
1189         ymax = self.convert_yunits(ymax) 
1190  
1191         if not np.iterable(x): 
1192             x = [x] 
1193         if not np.iterable(ymin): 
1194             ymin = [ymin] 
1195         if not np.iterable(ymax): 
1196             ymax = [ymax] 
1197  
1198         x, ymin, ymax = cbook.delete_masked_points(x, ymin, ymax) 
1199  
1200         x = np.ravel(x) 
1201         ymin = np.resize(ymin, x.shape) 
1202         ymax = np.resize(ymax, x.shape) 
1203  
1204         verts = [((thisx, thisymin), (thisx, thisymax)) 
1205                  for thisx, thisymin, thisymax in zip(x, ymin, ymax)] 
1206         lines = mcoll.LineCollection(verts, colors=colors, 
1207                                      linestyles=linestyles, label=label) 
1208         self.add_collection(lines, autolim=False) 
1209         lines.update(kwargs) 
1210  
1211         if len(x) > 0: 
1212             minx = x.min() 
1213             maxx = x.max() 
1214             miny = min(ymin.min(), ymax.min()) 
1215             maxy = max(ymin.max(), ymax.max()) 
1216  
1217             corners = (minx, miny), (maxx, maxy) 
1218             self.update_datalim(corners) 
1219             self._request_autoscale_view() 
1220  
1221         return lines

1223     @_preprocess_data(replace_names=["positions", "lineoffsets", 
1224                                      "linelengths", "linewidths", 
1225                                      "colors", "linestyles"]) 
1226     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
1227     def eventplot(self, positions, orientation='horizontal', lineoffsets=1, 
1228                   linelengths=1, linewidths=None, colors=None, 
1229                   linestyles='solid', **kwargs): 
1230         """ 
1231         Plot identical parallel lines at the given positions. 
1232  
1233         *positions* should be a 1D or 2D array-like object, with each row 
1234         corresponding to a row or column of lines. 
1235  
1236         This type of plot is commonly used in neuroscience for representing 
1237         neural events, where it is usually called a spike raster, dot raster, 
1238         or raster plot. 
1239  
1240         However, it is useful in any situation where you wish to show the 
1241         timing or position of multiple sets of discrete events, such as the 
1242         arrival times of people to a business on each day of the month or the 
1243         date of hurricanes each year of the last century. 
1244  
1245         Parameters 
1246         ---------- 
1247         positions : 1D or 2D array-like object 
1248             Each value is an event. If *positions* is a 2D array-like, each 
1249             row corresponds to a row or a column of lines (depending on the 
1250             *orientation* parameter). 
1251  
1252         orientation : {'horizontal', 'vertical'}, optional 
1253             The direction of the event collections: 
1254  
1255             - 'horizontal': the lines are arranged horizontally in rows, 
1256               and are vertical. 
1257             - 'vertical': the lines are arranged vertically in columns, 
1258               and are horizontal. 
1259  
1260         lineoffsets : scalar or sequence of scalars, default: 1 
1261             The offset of the center of the lines from the origin, in the 
1262             direction orthogonal to *orientation*. 
1263  
1264         linelengths : scalar or sequence of scalars, default: 1 
1265             The total height of the lines (i.e. the lines stretches from 
1266             ``lineoffset - linelength/2`` to ``lineoffset + linelength/2``). 
1267  
1268         linewidths : scalar, scalar sequence or None, default: None 
1269             The line width(s) of the event lines, in points. If it is None, 
1270             defaults to its rcParams setting. 
1271  
1272         colors : color, sequence of colors or None, default: None 
1273             The color(s) of the event lines. If it is None, defaults to its 
1274             rcParams setting. 
1275  
1276         linestyles : str or tuple or a sequence of such values, optional 
1277             Default is 'solid'. Valid strings are ['solid', 'dashed', 
1278             'dashdot', 'dotted', '-', '--', '-.', ':']. Dash tuples 
1279             should be of the form:: 
1280  
1281                 (offset, onoffseq), 
1282  
1283             where *onoffseq* is an even length tuple of on and off ink 
1284             in points. 
1285  
1286         **kwargs : optional 
1287             Other keyword arguments are line collection properties.  See 
1288             :class:`~matplotlib.collections.LineCollection` for a list of 
1289             the valid properties. 
1290  
1291         Returns 
1292         ------- 
1293         list : A list of :class:`~.collections.EventCollection` objects. 
1294             Contains the :class:`~.collections.EventCollection` that 
1295             were added. 
1296  
1297         Notes 
1298         ----- 
1299         For *linelengths*, *linewidths*, *colors*, and *linestyles*, if only 
1300         a single value is given, that value is applied to all lines.  If an 
1301         array-like is given, it must have the same length as *positions*, and 
1302         each value will be applied to the corresponding row of the array. 
1303  
1304         Examples 
1305         -------- 
1306         .. plot:: gallery/lines_bars_and_markers/eventplot_demo.py 
1307         """ 
1308         self._process_unit_info(xdata=positions, 
1309                                 ydata=[lineoffsets, linelengths], 
1310                                 kwargs=kwargs) 
1311  
1312         # We do the conversion first since not all unitized data is uniform 
1313         positions = self.convert_xunits(positions) 
1314         lineoffsets = self.convert_yunits(lineoffsets) 
1315         linelengths = self.convert_yunits(linelengths) 
1316  
1317         if not np.iterable(positions): 
1318             positions = [positions] 
1319         elif any(np.iterable(position) for position in positions): 
1320             positions = [np.asanyarray(position) for position in positions] 
1321         else: 
1322             positions = [np.asanyarray(positions)] 
1323  
1324         if len(positions) == 0: 
1325             return [] 
1326  
1327         # prevent 'singular' keys from **kwargs dict from overriding the effect 
1328         # of 'plural' keyword arguments (e.g. 'color' overriding 'colors') 
1329         colors = cbook.local_over_kwdict(colors, kwargs, 'color') 
1330         linewidths = cbook.local_over_kwdict(linewidths, kwargs, 'linewidth') 
1331         linestyles = cbook.local_over_kwdict(linestyles, kwargs, 'linestyle') 
1332  
1333         if not np.iterable(lineoffsets): 
1334             lineoffsets = [lineoffsets] 
1335         if not np.iterable(linelengths): 
1336             linelengths = [linelengths] 
1337         if not np.iterable(linewidths): 
1338             linewidths = [linewidths] 
1339         if not np.iterable(colors): 
1340             colors = [colors] 
1341         if hasattr(linestyles, 'lower') or not np.iterable(linestyles): 
1342             linestyles = [linestyles] 
1343  
1344         lineoffsets = np.asarray(lineoffsets) 
1345         linelengths = np.asarray(linelengths) 
1346         linewidths = np.asarray(linewidths) 
1347  
1348         if len(lineoffsets) == 0: 
1349             lineoffsets = [None] 
1350         if len(linelengths) == 0: 
1351             linelengths = [None] 
1352         if len(linewidths) == 0: 
1353             lineoffsets = [None] 
1354         if len(linewidths) == 0: 
1355             lineoffsets = [None] 
1356         if len(colors) == 0: 
1357             colors = [None] 
1358         try: 
1359             # Early conversion of the colors into RGBA values to take care 
1360             # of cases like colors='0.5' or colors='C1'.  (Issue #8193) 
1361             colors = mcolors.to_rgba_array(colors) 
1362         except ValueError: 
1363             # Will fail if any element of *colors* is None. But as long 
1364             # as len(colors) == 1 or len(positions), the rest of the 
1365             # code should process *colors* properly. 
1366             pass 
1367  
1368         if len(lineoffsets) == 1 and len(positions) != 1: 
1369             lineoffsets = np.tile(lineoffsets, len(positions)) 
1370             lineoffsets[0] = 0 
1371             lineoffsets = np.cumsum(lineoffsets) 
1372         if len(linelengths) == 1: 
1373             linelengths = np.tile(linelengths, len(positions)) 
1374         if len(linewidths) == 1: 
1375             linewidths = np.tile(linewidths, len(positions)) 
1376         if len(colors) == 1: 
1377             colors = list(colors) 
1378             colors = colors * len(positions) 
1379         if len(linestyles) == 1: 
1380             linestyles = [linestyles] * len(positions) 
1381  
1382         if len(lineoffsets) != len(positions): 
1383             raise ValueError('lineoffsets and positions are unequal sized ' 
1384                              'sequences') 
1385         if len(linelengths) != len(positions): 
1386             raise ValueError('linelengths and positions are unequal sized ' 
1387                              'sequences') 
1388         if len(linewidths) != len(positions): 
1389             raise ValueError('linewidths and positions are unequal sized ' 
1390                              'sequences') 
1391         if len(colors) != len(positions): 
1392             raise ValueError('colors and positions are unequal sized ' 
1393                              'sequences') 
1394         if len(linestyles) != len(positions): 
1395             raise ValueError('linestyles and positions are unequal sized ' 
1396                              'sequences') 
1397  
1398         colls = [] 
1399         for position, lineoffset, linelength, linewidth, color, linestyle in \ 
1400             zip(positions, lineoffsets, linelengths, linewidths, 
1401                            colors, linestyles): 
1402             coll = mcoll.EventCollection(position, 
1403                                          orientation=orientation, 
1404                                          lineoffset=lineoffset, 
1405                                          linelength=linelength, 
1406                                          linewidth=linewidth, 
1407                                          color=color, 
1408                                          linestyle=linestyle) 
1409             self.add_collection(coll, autolim=False) 
1410             coll.update(kwargs) 
1411             colls.append(coll) 
1412  
1413         if len(positions) > 0: 
1414             # try to get min/max 
1415             min_max = [(np.min(_p), np.max(_p)) for _p in positions 
1416                        if len(_p) > 0] 
1417             # if we have any non-empty positions, try to autoscale 
1418             if len(min_max) > 0: 
1419                 mins, maxes = zip(*min_max) 
1420                 minpos = np.min(mins) 
1421                 maxpos = np.max(maxes) 
1422  
1423                 minline = (lineoffsets - linelengths).min() 
1424                 maxline = (lineoffsets + linelengths).max() 
1425  
1426                 if (orientation is not None and 
1427                         orientation.lower() == "vertical"): 
1428                     corners = (minline, minpos), (maxline, maxpos) 
1429                 else:  # "horizontal", None or "none" (see EventCollection) 
1430                     corners = (minpos, minline), (maxpos, maxline) 
1431                 self.update_datalim(corners) 
1432                 self._request_autoscale_view() 
1433  
1434         return colls 
1435  
1436     #### Basic plotting 
1437  
1438     # Uses a custom implementation of data-kwarg handling in 
1439     # _process_plot_var_args. 
1440     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
1441     def plot(self, *args, scalex=True, scaley=True, data=None, **kwargs): 
1442         """ 
1443         Plot y versus x as lines and/or markers. 
1444  
1445         Call signatures:: 
1446  
1447             plot([x], y, [fmt], *, data=None, **kwargs) 
1448             plot([x], y, [fmt], [x2], y2, [fmt2], ..., **kwargs) 
1449  
1450         The coordinates of the points or line nodes are given by *x*, *y*. 
1451  
1452         The optional parameter *fmt* is a convenient way for defining basic 
1453         formatting like color, marker and linestyle. It's a shortcut string 
1454         notation described in the *Notes* section below. 
1455  
1456         >>> plot(x, y)        # plot x and y using default line style and color 
1457         >>> plot(x, y, 'bo')  # plot x and y using blue circle markers 
1458         >>> plot(y)           # plot y using x as index array 0..N-1 
1459         >>> plot(y, 'r+')     # ditto, but with red plusses 
1460  
1461         You can use `.Line2D` properties as keyword arguments for more 
1462         control on the appearance. Line properties and *fmt* can be mixed. 
1463         The following two calls yield identical results: 
1464  
1465         >>> plot(x, y, 'go--', linewidth=2, markersize=12) 
1466         >>> plot(x, y, color='green', marker='o', linestyle='dashed', 
1467         ...      linewidth=2, markersize=12) 
1468  
1469         When conflicting with *fmt*, keyword arguments take precedence. 
1470  
1471  
1472         **Plotting labelled data** 
1473  
1474         There's a convenient way for plotting objects with labelled data (i.e. 
1475         data that can be accessed by index ``obj['y']``). Instead of giving 
1476         the data in *x* and *y*, you can provide the object in the *data* 
1477         parameter and just give the labels for *x* and *y*:: 
1478  
1479         >>> plot('xlabel', 'ylabel', data=obj) 
1480  
1481         All indexable objects are supported. This could e.g. be a `dict`, a 
1482         `pandas.DataFame` or a structured numpy array. 
1483  
1484  
1485         **Plotting multiple sets of data** 
1486  
1487         There are various ways to plot multiple sets of data. 
1488  
1489         - The most straight forward way is just to call `plot` multiple times. 
1490           Example: 
1491  
1492           >>> plot(x1, y1, 'bo') 
1493           >>> plot(x2, y2, 'go') 
1494  
1495         - Alternatively, if your data is already a 2d array, you can pass it 
1496           directly to *x*, *y*. A separate data set will be drawn for every 
1497           column. 
1498  
1499           Example: an array ``a`` where the first column represents the *x* 
1500           values and the other columns are the *y* columns:: 
1501  
1502           >>> plot(a[0], a[1:]) 
1503  
1504         - The third way is to specify multiple sets of *[x]*, *y*, *[fmt]* 
1505           groups:: 
1506  
1507           >>> plot(x1, y1, 'g^', x2, y2, 'g-') 
1508  
1509           In this case, any additional keyword argument applies to all 
1510           datasets. Also this syntax cannot be combined with the *data* 
1511           parameter. 
1512  
1513         By default, each line is assigned a different style specified by a 
1514         'style cycle'. The *fmt* and line property parameters are only 
1515         necessary if you want explicit deviations from these defaults. 
1516         Alternatively, you can also change the style cycle using 
1517         :rc:`axes.prop_cycle`. 
1518  
1519  
1520         Parameters 
1521         ---------- 
1522         x, y : array-like or scalar 
1523             The horizontal / vertical coordinates of the data points. 
1524             *x* values are optional and default to ``range(len(y))``. 
1525  
1526             Commonly, these parameters are 1D arrays. 
1527  
1528             They can also be scalars, or two-dimensional (in that case, the 
1529             columns represent separate data sets). 
1530  
1531             These arguments cannot be passed as keywords. 
1532  
1533         fmt : str, optional 
1534             A format string, e.g. 'ro' for red circles. See the *Notes* 
1535             section for a full description of the format strings. 
1536  
1537             Format strings are just an abbreviation for quickly setting 
1538             basic line properties. All of these and more can also be 
1539             controlled by keyword arguments. 
1540  
1541             This argument cannot be passed as keyword. 
1542  
1543         data : indexable object, optional 
1544             An object with labelled data. If given, provide the label names to 
1545             plot in *x* and *y*. 
1546  
1547             .. note:: 
1548                 Technically there's a slight ambiguity in calls where the 
1549                 second label is a valid *fmt*. ``plot('n', 'o', data=obj)`` 
1550                 could be ``plt(x, y)`` or ``plt(y, fmt)``. In such cases, 
1551                 the former interpretation is chosen, but a warning is issued. 
1552                 You may suppress the warning by adding an empty format string 
1553                 ``plot('n', 'o', '', data=obj)``. 
1554  
1555         Other Parameters 
1556         ---------------- 
1557         scalex, scaley : bool, default: True 
1558             These parameters determined if the view limits are adapted to 
1559             the data limits. The values are passed on to `autoscale_view`. 
1560  
1561         **kwargs : `.Line2D` properties, optional 
1562             *kwargs* are used to specify properties like a line label (for 
1563             auto legends), linewidth, antialiasing, marker face color. 
1564             Example:: 
1565  
1566             >>> plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], 'go-', label='line 1', linewidth=2) 
1567             >>> plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], 'rs', label='line 2') 
1568  
1569             If you make multiple lines with one plot command, the kwargs 
1570             apply to all those lines. 
1571  
1572             Here is a list of available `.Line2D` properties: 
1573  
1574             %(_Line2D_docstr)s 
1575  
1576         Returns 
1577         ------- 
1578         lines 
1579             A list of `.Line2D` objects representing the plotted data. 
1580  
1581         See Also 
1582         -------- 
1583         scatter : XY scatter plot with markers of varying size and/or color ( 
1584             sometimes also called bubble chart). 
1585  
1586         Notes 
1587         ----- 
1588         **Format Strings** 
1589  
1590         A format string consists of a part for color, marker and line:: 
1591  
1592             fmt = '[marker][line][color]' 
1593  
1594         Each of them is optional. If not provided, the value from the style 
1595         cycle is used. Exception: If ``line`` is given, but no ``marker``, 
1596         the data will be a line without markers. 
1597  
1598         Other combinations such as ``[color][marker][line]`` are also 
1599         supported, but note that their parsing may be ambiguous. 
1600  
1601         **Markers** 
1602  
1603         =============    =============================== 
1604         character        description 
1605         =============    =============================== 
1606         ``'.'``          point marker 
1607         ``','``          pixel marker 
1608         ``'o'``          circle marker 
1609         ``'v'``          triangle_down marker 
1610         ``'^'``          triangle_up marker 
1611         ``'<'``          triangle_left marker 
1612         ``'>'``          triangle_right marker 
1613         ``'1'``          tri_down marker 
1614         ``'2'``          tri_up marker 
1615         ``'3'``          tri_left marker 
1616         ``'4'``          tri_right marker 
1617         ``'s'``          square marker 
1618         ``'p'``          pentagon marker 
1619         ``'*'``          star marker 
1620         ``'h'``          hexagon1 marker 
1621         ``'H'``          hexagon2 marker 
1622         ``'+'``          plus marker 
1623         ``'x'``          x marker 
1624         ``'D'``          diamond marker 
1625         ``'d'``          thin_diamond marker 
1626         ``'|'``          vline marker 
1627         ``'_'``          hline marker 
1628         =============    =============================== 
1629  
1630         **Line Styles** 
1631  
1632         =============    =============================== 
1633         character        description 
1634         =============    =============================== 
1635         ``'-'``          solid line style 
1636         ``'--'``         dashed line style 
1637         ``'-.'``         dash-dot line style 
1638         ``':'``          dotted line style 
1639         =============    =============================== 
1640  
1641         Example format strings:: 
1642  
1643             'b'    # blue markers with default shape 
1644             'or'   # red circles 
1645             '-g'   # green solid line 
1646             '--'   # dashed line with default color 
1647             '^k:'  # black triangle_up markers connected by a dotted line 
1648  
1649         **Colors** 
1650  
1651         The supported color abbreviations are the single letter codes 
1652  
1653         =============    =============================== 
1654         character        color 
1655         =============    =============================== 
1656         ``'b'``          blue 
1657         ``'g'``          green 
1658         ``'r'``          red 
1659         ``'c'``          cyan 
1660         ``'m'``          magenta 
1661         ``'y'``          yellow 
1662         ``'k'``          black 
1663         ``'w'``          white 
1664         =============    =============================== 
1665  
1666         and the ``'CN'`` colors that index into the default property cycle. 
1667  
1668         If the color is the only part of the format string, you can 
1669         additionally use any  `matplotlib.colors` spec, e.g. full names 
1670         (``'green'``) or hex strings (``'#008000'``). 
1671         """ 
1672         kwargs = cbook.normalize_kwargs(kwargs, mlines.Line2D) 
1673         lines = [*self._get_lines(*args, data=data, **kwargs)] 
1674         for line in lines: 
1675             self.add_line(line) 
1676         self._request_autoscale_view(scalex=scalex, scaley=scaley) 
1677         return lines 
1678  
1679     @_preprocess_data(replace_names=["x", "y"], label_namer="y") 
1680     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
1681     def plot_date(self, x, y, fmt='o', tz=None, xdate=True, ydate=False, 
1682                   **kwargs): 
1683         """ 
1684         Plot data that contains dates. 
1685  
1686         Similar to `.plot`, this plots *y* vs. *x* as lines or markers. 
1687         However, the axis labels are formatted as dates depending on *xdate* 
1688         and *ydate*. 
1689  
1690         Parameters 
1691         ---------- 
1692         x, y : array-like 
1693             The coordinates of the data points. If *xdate* or *ydate* is 
1694             *True*, the respective values *x* or *y* are interpreted as 
1695             :ref:`Matplotlib dates <date-format>`. 
1696  
1697         fmt : str, optional 
1698             The plot format string. For details, see the corresponding 
1699             parameter in `.plot`. 
1700  
1701         tz : timezone string or `tzinfo` or None 
1702             The time zone to use in labeling dates. If *None*, defaults to 
1703             :rc:`timezone`. 
1704  
1705         xdate : bool, default: True 
1706             If *True*, the *x*-axis will be interpreted as Matplotlib dates. 
1707  
1708         ydate : bool, default: False 
1709             If *True*, the *y*-axis will be interpreted as Matplotlib dates. 
1710  
1711  
1712         Returns 
1713         ------- 
1714         lines 
1715             A list of `.Line2D` objects representing the plotted data. 
1716  
1717  
1718         Other Parameters 
1719         ---------------- 
1720         **kwargs 
1721             Keyword arguments control the `.Line2D` properties: 
1722  
1723             %(_Line2D_docstr)s 
1724  
1725         See Also 
1726         -------- 
1727         matplotlib.dates : Helper functions on dates. 
1728         matplotlib.dates.date2num : Convert dates to num. 
1729         matplotlib.dates.num2date : Convert num to dates. 
1730         matplotlib.dates.drange : Create an equally spaced sequence of dates. 
1731  
1732         Notes 
1733         ----- 
1734         If you are using custom date tickers and formatters, it may be 
1735         necessary to set the formatters/locators after the call to 
1736         `.plot_date`. `.plot_date` will set the default tick locator to 
1737         `.AutoDateLocator` (if the tick locator is not already set to a 
1738         `.DateLocator` instance) and the default tick formatter to 
1739         `.AutoDateFormatter` (if the tick formatter is not already set to a 
1740         `.DateFormatter` instance). 
1741         """ 
1742         if xdate: 
1743             self.xaxis_date(tz) 
1744         if ydate: 
1745             self.yaxis_date(tz) 
1746  
1747         ret = self.plot(x, y, fmt, **kwargs) 
1748  
1749         self._request_autoscale_view() 
1750  
1751         return ret

1753     # @_preprocess_data() # let 'plot' do the unpacking.. 
1754     @docstring.dedent_interpd 
1755     def loglog(self, *args, **kwargs): 
1756         """ 
1757         Make a plot with log scaling on both the x and y axis. 
1758  
1759         Call signatures:: 
1760  
1761             loglog([x], y, [fmt], data=None, **kwargs) 
1762             loglog([x], y, [fmt], [x2], y2, [fmt2], ..., **kwargs) 
1763  
1764         This is just a thin wrapper around `.plot` which additionally changes 
1765         both the x-axis and the y-axis to log scaling. All of the concepts and 
1766         parameters of plot can be used here as well. 
1767  
1768         The additional parameters *basex/y*, *subsx/y* and *nonposx/y* control 
1769         the x/y-axis properties. They are just forwarded to `.Axes.set_xscale` 
1770         and `.Axes.set_yscale`. 
1771  
1772         Parameters 
1773         ---------- 
1774         basex, basey : scalar, optional, default 10 
1775             Base of the x/y logarithm. 
1776  
1777         subsx, subsy : sequence, optional 
1778             The location of the minor x/y ticks. If *None*, reasonable 
1779             locations are automatically chosen depending on the number of 
1780             decades in the plot. 
1781             See `.Axes.set_xscale` / `.Axes.set_yscale` for details. 
1782  
1783         nonposx, nonposy : {'mask', 'clip'}, optional, default 'mask' 
1784             Non-positive values in x or y can be masked as invalid, or clipped 
1785             to a very small positive number. 
1786  
1787         Returns 
1788         ------- 
1789         lines 
1790             A list of `.Line2D` objects representing the plotted data. 
1791  
1792         Other Parameters 
1793         ---------------- 
1794         **kwargs 
1795             All parameters supported by `.plot`. 
1796         """ 
1797         dx = {k: kwargs.pop(k) for k in ['basex', 'subsx', 'nonposx'] 
1798               if k in kwargs} 
1799         dy = {k: kwargs.pop(k) for k in ['basey', 'subsy', 'nonposy'] 
1800               if k in kwargs} 
1801  
1802         self.set_xscale('log', **dx) 
1803         self.set_yscale('log', **dy) 
1804  
1805         l = self.plot(*args, **kwargs) 
1806         return l

1906     @_preprocess_data(replace_names=["x"], label_namer="x") 
1907     def acorr(self, x, **kwargs): 
1908         """ 
1909         Plot the autocorrelation of *x*. 
1910  
1911         Parameters 
1912         ---------- 
1913         x : array-like 
1914  
1915         detrend : callable, default: `mlab.detrend_none` 
1916             *x* is detrended by the *detrend* callable. This must be a 
1917             function ``x = detrend(x)`` accepting and returning an 
1918             `numpy.array`. Default is no detrending. 
1919  
1920         normed : bool, default: True 
1921             If ``True``, input vectors are normalised to unit length. 
1922  
1923         usevlines : bool, default: True 
1924             Determines the plot style. 
1925  
1926             If ``True``, vertical lines are plotted from 0 to the acorr value 
1927             using `Axes.vlines`. Additionally, a horizontal line is plotted 
1928             at y=0 using `Axes.axhline`. 
1929  
1930             If ``False``, markers are plotted at the acorr values using 
1931             `Axes.plot`. 
1932  
1933         maxlags : int, default: 10 
1934             Number of lags to show. If ``None``, will return all 
1935             ``2 * len(x) - 1`` lags. 
1936  
1937         Returns 
1938         ------- 
1939         lags : array (length ``2*maxlags+1``) 
1940             The lag vector. 
1941         c : array  (length ``2*maxlags+1``) 
1942             The auto correlation vector. 
1943         line : `.LineCollection` or `.Line2D` 
1944             `.Artist` added to the axes of the correlation: 
1945  
1946             - `.LineCollection` if *usevlines* is True. 
1947             - `.Line2D` if *usevlines* is False. 
1948         b : `.Line2D` or None 
1949             Horizontal line at 0 if *usevlines* is True 
1950             None *usevlines* is False. 
1951  
1952         Other Parameters 
1953         ---------------- 
1954         linestyle : `.Line2D` property, optional 
1955             The linestyle for plotting the data points. 
1956             Only used if *usevlines* is ``False``. 
1957  
1958         marker : str, default: 'o' 
1959             The marker for plotting the data points. 
1960             Only used if *usevlines* is ``False``. 
1961  
1962         Notes 
1963         ----- 
1964         The cross correlation is performed with :func:`numpy.correlate` with 
1965         ``mode = "full"``. 
1966         """ 
1967         return self.xcorr(x, x, **kwargs) 
1968  
1969     @_preprocess_data(replace_names=["x", "y"], label_namer="y") 
1970     def xcorr(self, x, y, normed=True, detrend=mlab.detrend_none, 
1971               usevlines=True, maxlags=10, **kwargs): 
1972         r""" 
1973         Plot the cross correlation between *x* and *y*. 
1974  
1975         The correlation with lag k is defined as 
1976         :math:`\sum_n x[n+k] \cdot y^*[n]`, where :math:`y^*` is the complex 
1977         conjugate of :math:`y`. 
1978  
1979         Parameters 
1980         ---------- 
1981         x : array-like of length n 
1982  
1983         y : array-like of length n 
1984  
1985         detrend : callable, default: `mlab.detrend_none` 
1986             *x* and *y* are detrended by the *detrend* callable. This must be a 
1987             function ``x = detrend(x)`` accepting and returning an 
1988             `numpy.array`. Default is no detrending. 
1989  
1990         normed : bool, default: True 
1991             If ``True``, input vectors are normalised to unit length. 
1992  
1993         usevlines : bool, default: True 
1994             Determines the plot style. 
1995  
1996             If ``True``, vertical lines are plotted from 0 to the xcorr value 
1997             using `Axes.vlines`. Additionally, a horizontal line is plotted 
1998             at y=0 using `Axes.axhline`. 
1999  
2000             If ``False``, markers are plotted at the xcorr values using 
2001             `Axes.plot`. 
2002  
2003         maxlags : int, default: 10 
2004             Number of lags to show. If None, will return all ``2 * len(x) - 1`` 
2005             lags. 
2006  
2007         Returns 
2008         ------- 
2009         lags : array (length ``2*maxlags+1``) 
2010             The lag vector. 
2011         c : array  (length ``2*maxlags+1``) 
2012             The auto correlation vector. 
2013         line : `.LineCollection` or `.Line2D` 
2014             `.Artist` added to the axes of the correlation: 
2015  
2016             - `.LineCollection` if *usevlines* is True. 
2017             - `.Line2D` if *usevlines* is False. 
2018         b : `.Line2D` or None 
2019             Horizontal line at 0 if *usevlines* is True 
2020             None *usevlines* is False. 
2021  
2022         Other Parameters 
2023         ---------------- 
2024         linestyle : `.Line2D` property, optional 
2025             The linestyle for plotting the data points. 
2026             Only used if *usevlines* is ``False``. 
2027  
2028         marker : str, default: 'o' 
2029             The marker for plotting the data points. 
2030             Only used if *usevlines* is ``False``. 
2031  
2032         Notes 
2033         ----- 
2034         The cross correlation is performed with :func:`numpy.correlate` with 
2035         ``mode = "full"``. 
2036         """ 
2037         Nx = len(x) 
2038         if Nx != len(y): 
2039             raise ValueError('x and y must be equal length') 
2040  
2041         x = detrend(np.asarray(x)) 
2042         y = detrend(np.asarray(y)) 
2043  
2044         correls = np.correlate(x, y, mode="full") 
2045  
2046         if normed: 
2047             correls /= np.sqrt(np.dot(x, x) * np.dot(y, y)) 
2048  
2049         if maxlags is None: 
2050             maxlags = Nx - 1 
2051  
2052         if maxlags >= Nx or maxlags < 1: 
2053             raise ValueError('maxlags must be None or strictly ' 
2054                              'positive < %d' % Nx) 
2055  
2056         lags = np.arange(-maxlags, maxlags + 1) 
2057         correls = correls[Nx - 1 - maxlags:Nx + maxlags] 
2058  
2059         if usevlines: 
2060             a = self.vlines(lags, [0], correls, **kwargs) 
2061             # Make label empty so only vertical lines get a legend entry 
2062             kwargs.pop('label', '') 
2063             b = self.axhline(**kwargs) 
2064         else: 
2065             kwargs.setdefault('marker', 'o') 
2066             kwargs.setdefault('linestyle', 'None') 
2067             a, = self.plot(lags, correls, **kwargs) 
2068             b = None 
2069         return lags, correls, a, b

2073     # @_preprocess_data() # let 'plot' do the unpacking.. 
2074     def step(self, x, y, *args, where='pre', data=None, **kwargs): 
2075         """ 
2076         Make a step plot. 
2077  
2078         Call signatures:: 
2079  
2080             step(x, y, [fmt], *, data=None, where='pre', **kwargs) 
2081             step(x, y, [fmt], x2, y2, [fmt2], ..., *, where='pre', **kwargs) 
2082  
2083         This is just a thin wrapper around `.plot` which changes some 
2084         formatting options. Most of the concepts and parameters of plot can be 
2085         used here as well. 
2086  
2087         Parameters 
2088         ---------- 
2089         x : array-like 
2090             1-D sequence of x positions. It is assumed, but not checked, that 
2091             it is uniformly increasing. 
2092  
2093         y : array-like 
2094             1-D sequence of y levels. 
2095  
2096         fmt : str, optional 
2097             A format string, e.g. 'g' for a green line. See `.plot` for a more 
2098             detailed description. 
2099  
2100             Note: While full format strings are accepted, it is recommended to 
2101             only specify the color. Line styles are currently ignored (use 
2102             the keyword argument *linestyle* instead). Markers are accepted 
2103             and plotted on the given positions, however, this is a rarely 
2104             needed feature for step plots. 
2105  
2106         data : indexable object, optional 
2107             An object with labelled data. If given, provide the label names to 
2108             plot in *x* and *y*. 
2109  
2110         where : {'pre', 'post', 'mid'}, default: 'pre' 
2111             Define where the steps should be placed: 
2112  
2113             - 'pre': The y value is continued constantly to the left from 
2114               every *x* position, i.e. the interval ``(x[i-1], x[i]]`` has the 
2115               value ``y[i]``. 
2116             - 'post': The y value is continued constantly to the right from 
2117               every *x* position, i.e. the interval ``[x[i], x[i+1])`` has the 
2118               value ``y[i]``. 
2119             - 'mid': Steps occur half-way between the *x* positions. 
2120  
2121         Returns 
2122         ------- 
2123         lines 
2124             A list of `.Line2D` objects representing the plotted data. 
2125  
2126         Other Parameters 
2127         ---------------- 
2128         **kwargs 
2129             Additional parameters are the same as those for `.plot`. 
2130  
2131         Notes 
2132         ----- 
2133         .. [notes section required to get data note injection right] 
2134         """ 
2135         cbook._check_in_list(('pre', 'post', 'mid'), where=where) 
2136         kwargs['drawstyle'] = 'steps-' + where 
2137         return self.plot(x, y, *args, data=data, **kwargs)

2139     @staticmethod 
2140     def _convert_dx(dx, x0, xconv, convert): 
2141         """ 
2142         Small helper to do logic of width conversion flexibly. 
2143  
2144         *dx* and *x0* have units, but *xconv* has already been converted 
2145         to unitless (and is an ndarray).  This allows the *dx* to have units 
2146         that are different from *x0*, but are still accepted by the 
2147         ``__add__`` operator of *x0*. 
2148         """ 
2149  
2150         # x should be an array... 
2151         assert type(xconv) is np.ndarray 
2152  
2153         if xconv.size == 0: 
2154             # xconv has already been converted, but maybe empty... 
2155             return convert(dx) 
2156  
2157         try: 
2158             # attempt to add the width to x0; this works for 
2159             # datetime+timedelta, for instance 
2160  
2161             # only use the first element of x and x0.  This saves 
2162             # having to be sure addition works across the whole 
2163             # vector.  This is particularly an issue if 
2164             # x0 and dx are lists so x0 + dx just concatenates the lists. 
2165             # We can't just cast x0 and dx to numpy arrays because that 
2166             # removes the units from unit packages like `pint` that 
2167             # wrap numpy arrays. 
2168             try: 
2169                 x0 = cbook.safe_first_element(x0) 
2170             except (TypeError, IndexError, KeyError): 
2171                 x0 = x0 
2172  
2173             try: 
2174                 x = cbook.safe_first_element(xconv) 
2175             except (TypeError, IndexError, KeyError): 
2176                 x = xconv 
2177  
2178             delist = False 
2179             if not np.iterable(dx): 
2180                 dx = [dx] 
2181                 delist = True 
2182             dx = [convert(x0 + ddx) - x for ddx in dx] 
2183             if delist: 
2184                 dx = dx[0] 
2185         except (ValueError, TypeError, AttributeError): 
2186             # if the above fails (for any reason) just fallback to what 
2187             # we do by default and convert dx by itself. 
2188             dx = convert(dx) 
2189         return dx
